TcpStack: one BuildSegment builds the connection's five kinds of segment - data, fast retransmit, FIN, zero-window probe, RST - where five blocks set the header field by field; the flags are one store of the wire bits, where the setters made a read-modify-write each, and the data segment is built after the lock like the others; a test checks that a write's segments all carry ACK and only the last one PSH (Opus max review taken, two rounds)

TcpStack: the receive window is ReceiveWindow, a class of its own with its own tests - the pipe the stream reads, the unread count, the window last advertised and the window-update rule (a closed window reopened to 4096 bytes, or opened by a quarter since the last advertisement) - where eight members of the connection held it; Dispose completes the pipe under its lock, so the receive path needs no disposed check of its own; a write past the window throws, and the connection logs it and resets; the iOS memory doc names the new members; 80 MB through 40 flows as fast as before, the same peak memory (Opus max review taken, two rounds; the kernel-path tests run on a VM)

TcpStack: the retransmit ring is RetransmitBuffer, a class of its own with its own tests - Append, Trim and the copy of the front for a retransmission, allocated on the first send as before - where four fields and two helpers of the connection held it; an overflow, a Debug.Assert before (nothing in Release: the retransmitted bytes silently corrupted), is refused with an exception, and both senders append before they advance SndNxt, so a refused segment changes nothing; the test project sees the stack's internals (Opus max review taken, two rounds)
